error_modes.label: Takeoff airspeed control and rotation point

texts.0: SP, due to an imprecise power application and a late reference to the calculated takeoff data, did not execute the T/O with the standard airspeed. Rotation was withheld well past the computed point and the aircraft was flown off more than 10 knots above the standard takeoff airspeed, outside the -0,+10 knots tolerance. The fast condition was not recognized and the acceleration continued unchecked. IP intervened with a directive call to rotate and set the takeoff attitude before the remaining runway became a factor.
texts.1: SP, due to a hesitant rotation input at the computed speed, did not execute the T/O with the standard airspeed. Liftoff occurred about 10 knots fast, at the limit of the -0,+10 knots tolerance. SP made no corrective input until the IP gave a verbal call, and the airspeed was brought back to the standard only after that prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed cross-check of the airspeed indication in the last part of the ground roll, did not rotate exactly at the standard takeoff airspeed. Liftoff occurred approximately 7 knots fast, between the -0,+5 and the -0,+10 knots tolerances. SP recognized the fast trend, set the takeoff attitude and contained the airspeed in time, with no IP intervention required.
texts.3: SP executed the T/O with the standard airspeed, cross-checking the airspeed indication against the calculated takeoff data throughout the ground roll. Rotation was initiated at the briefed speed and the airspeed at liftoff remained within the -0,+5 knots tolerance. Control inputs were smooth and no acceleration overshoot developed.
texts.4: SP executed the T/O with the standard airspeed and rotated precisely at the computed speed. Airspeed at liftoff showed negligible deviation from the standard takeoff airspeed, with no perceptible overshoot during the acceleration. The airspeed cross-check was continuous from brake release to liftoff and the calculated takeoff data were verified against actual aircraft performance.
texts.marginal: SP executed the T/O within the required airspeed tolerance, but rotation was consistently initiated a few knots late and the airspeed trended toward the upper edge of the standard on each attempt. No prompting was needed and every takeoff stayed within standards. SP is expected to tighten the airspeed cross-check in the final part of the ground roll so that rotation is initiated at the exact standard takeoff airspeed.

error_modes.label: Runway centerline tracking during takeoff roll
error_modes.source: specific:Maintain in the center line of RWY (ft)

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient and late rudder input against the crosswind component, did not maintain the A/C at the centerline during T/O. Lateral displacement exceeded 10 ft from the runway centerline, outside the +/-10 ft tolerance, and continued to diverge through liftoff. IP intervened on the controls to re-establish the takeoff track along the centerline.
texts.1: SP, due to directional corrections applied only after the drift had become visible, did not maintain the A/C at the centerline during T/O. Displacement reached about 10 ft from the runway centerline, at the limit of the +/-10 ft tolerance, and the track was recovered only after a verbal call from the IP. No anticipatory rudder input was made during the acceleration.
texts.2: SP, due to coarse rudder inputs made after the drift developed rather than as it began, did not hold the A/C precisely on the centerline during the takeoff roll. Displacement reached approximately 8 ft, between the +/-5 ft and the +/-10 ft tolerances. SP identified the divergence, applied the correct rudder and re-established the track before liftoff without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the A/C at the centerline during T/O, tracking within +/-5 ft from brake release to liftoff. Rudder inputs were small, anticipatory and matched to the crosswind component, and the aircraft was flown off with no lateral divergence. Directional control was maintained without any assistance from the IP.
texts.4: SP maintained the A/C at the centerline during T/O with negligible lateral displacement throughout the ground roll and at liftoff. Rudder inputs anticipated the crosswind and the yaw from power application, so no correcting input larger than trim-level was required. The takeoff track remained aligned with the runway centerline into the climb.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the A/C at the centerline within the required tolerance, but the aircraft drifted repeatedly to the same side of the runway centerline and every correction was reactive rather than anticipatory. All displacements remained inside +/-5 ft and no prompting was needed. SP is expected to lead the crosswind with rudder from brake release so that the drift is prevented rather than corrected.

error_modes.label: LINE UP checks completeness and sequence

texts.0: SP, due to a lapse in which a briefed item was omitted under workload, did not execute the LINE UP checks without omissions and did not accomplish the After Takeoff Checklist at the correct point. More than one required item was left unverified and the omission was still uncorrected after liftoff. IP intervened by directing that the checks be re-accomplished in flight before the departure was continued.
texts.1: SP, due to a lapse under the workload of the line-up sequence, did not execute the LINE UP checks without omissions. One required item was omitted and was recovered only after the IP prompted the check, with the takeoff roll already begun. SP had accepted the checks as complete without a verification pass.
texts.2: SP, due to an interrupted flow through the LINE UP checks after the takeoff clearance was received, did not complete the checks in the briefed sequence on the first pass. SP detected the skipped item on his own, completed it before brake release and required no IP intervention. The departure was not delayed and no item entered the takeoff roll unverified.
texts.3: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions and accomplished the After Takeoff Checklist at the correct point in the departure. Each item was verified against the actual switch position and indication rather than from memory. The flow was completed inside the time available on the runway without rushing.
texts.4: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions, in the published sequence and with each item confirmed against the corresponding indication. The After Takeoff Checklist was accomplished at the correct point with no interruption to aircraft control. Checklist discipline was maintained despite the radio and traffic activity present at the time.
texts.marginal: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions, but the flow was slow and a second scan was needed before SP was satisfied that the checks were complete. All items were verified and no prompting was required. SP is expected to consolidate the check flow so that it is completed in one pass and does not compete with lineup and directional control tasks.

error_modes.label: Brake hold and aircraft movement during engine run-up

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient brake pressure while advancing the PCL for the engine run-up, allowed movement of the A/C during the run-up. The aircraft crept forward before the run-up indications were checked and the run-up was not accomplished from a stationary position. IP intervened by directing the power to be retarded and the aircraft stopped before the takeoff was continued.
texts.1: SP, due to brake pressure that was relaxed as attention moved to the engine indications, allowed a continuous forward creep of the A/C during the run-up. The run-up parameters were checked while the aircraft was moving, and full brake pressure was reapplied only after the IP called the movement.
texts.2: SP, due to brake pressure applied slightly after the PCL was advanced, allowed a brief forward creep at the start of the engine run-up. SP recognized the movement immediately, arrested it with prompt brake application and completed the check of the run-up indications with the aircraft stationary. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP held the brakes firmly throughout the engine run-up and did not allow any movement of the A/C. Power was set and the engine indications were checked against the calculated takeoff data with the aircraft stationary on the centerline. Brake release was made only after the run-up check was complete.
texts.4: SP held full brake pressure before advancing the PCL and did not allow any movement of the A/C during the engine run-up. The run-up indications were checked deliberately and compared with the calculated takeoff data while the aircraft remained exactly on the centerline. Brake release and power application were then made as a single smooth sequence.
texts.marginal: SP did not allow any movement of the A/C during the engine run-up, but the brake pressure applied was only just sufficient and a slight relaxation was observed as attention shifted to the engine indications. The aircraft remained stationary and no prompting was needed. SP is expected to establish and hold positive brake pressure before the PCL is advanced so that the margin does not depend on attention.

texts.0: SP, due to an imprecise pitch input at rotation and no subsequent attitude reference, did not bring and maintain the A/C to the proper T/O attitude and did not establish the proper climbing attitude. The aircraft was flown off in a shallow attitude and the airspeed increased more than 10 knots beyond the standard, outside the -0,+10 knots tolerance, while the pitch continued to wander. IP intervened on the controls to set and hold the climb attitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a pitch input that was not stabilized against the attitude reference, did not maintain the proper T/O and climbing attitude after liftoff. The attitude oscillated and the airspeed reached about 10 knots off the standard, at the limit of the -0,+10 knots tolerance. The attitude was stabilized only after repeated verbal directions from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a pitch rate at rotation that was slightly high and then relaxed, did not hold the proper T/O attitude steady through the initial climb. The resulting airspeed excursion reached roughly 7 knots from the standard, between the -0,+5 and the -0,+10 knots tolerances. SP recognized the attitude error against the attitude reference and re-established the proper climbing attitude promptly, with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP brought and maintained the A/C to the proper T/O attitude at rotation and established the proper climbing attitude immediately after liftoff. The attitude was held steady against the attitude reference and the airspeed remained within the -0,+5 knots tolerance. No pitch oscillation developed during the transition to the climb.
texts.4: SP set the proper T/O attitude with a single smooth pitch input and transitioned directly to the proper climbing attitude with no intermediate correction. The attitude was held with negligible variation and the airspeed showed negligible deviation from the standard. Trim was used so that the climb attitude was maintained with light control forces.
texts.marginal: SP brought and maintained the A/C to the proper T/O and climbing attitude within standards, but the attitude was set through two or three small corrections rather than in one input and remained slightly unsteady in the first seconds of the climb. All resulting airspeed deviations stayed within the standard and no prompting was needed. SP is expected to set the target attitude in a single input and trim early so that the climb attitude is stable from liftoff.

texts.0: SP, due to workload distribution that left the SP flying and transmitting at the same time, did not clean the A/C configuration without violating the speed limit. L/G and flaps retraction was commanded after the aircraft had accelerated past the limiting speed for the configuration, and the exceedance was neither recognized nor reported. IP intervened by directing the pitch increase and the retraction sequence.
texts.1: SP, due to attention divided between the departure transmission and aircraft control, did not command the L/G and flaps retraction at the briefed point. The retraction was initiated right at the limiting speed for the configuration and only after a verbal reminder from the IP, leaving no margin to the speed limit.
texts.2: SP, due to a retraction sequence delayed by a few seconds while the departure call was made, did not clean the A/C configuration at the briefed point. The airspeed approached but did not reach the limiting speed for the configuration. SP recognized the accelerating trend, adjusted the pitch attitude and completed the L/G and flaps retraction in time, with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP cleaned the A/C configuration at the correct points in the departure and did not violate the speed limit for L/G or flaps. The retraction was sequenced with the climb attitude so that a comfortable margin to the limiting speeds was preserved, and the radio work was fitted between the control tasks.
texts.4: SP cleaned the A/C configuration exactly at the briefed points with a wide margin to the L/G and flaps limiting speeds. The retraction sequence, the attitude control and the departure transmission were separated in time so that no task competed with aircraft control. Configuration and indication checks were confirmed after each retraction.
texts.marginal: SP cleaned the A/C configuration without violating any speed limit, but the retractions were commanded consistently late and the margin to the limiting speeds was small on each occasion. Aircraft control was maintained and no prompting was required. SP is expected to sequence the retraction ahead of the departure transmission so that the configuration change is completed with a clear margin to the limiting speed.

error_modes.label: Acceleration to and maintenance of standard climb airspeed

texts.0: SP, due to a pitch attitude flown without reference to the airspeed trend, did not accelerate and maintain the proper climb airspeed after the configuration was clean. The airspeed diverged more than 10 knots from the standard climb airspeed, beyond the -0,+10 knots tolerance applied to the takeoff airspeed, and the divergence persisted into the departure. IP intervened on the controls to re-establish the standard climb airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to late and undersized pitch corrections, did not maintain the proper climb airspeed once the aircraft was clean. The airspeed settled about 10 knots off the standard climb airspeed, at the limit of the -0,+10 knots tolerance, and returned to the standard only after repeated verbal directions from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a pitch attitude set slightly low during the acceleration, did not stabilize on the standard climb airspeed at the briefed point. The airspeed deviation reached approximately 7 knots, between the -0,+5 and the -0,+10 knots tolerances. SP identified the deviation on the airspeed indication and corrected it with a measured pitch change, with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP accelerated the A/C to the standard climb airspeed and maintained it through the departure. Pitch was adjusted in small increments against the airspeed indication and the airspeed was held within the -0,+5 knots tolerance. Trim was set so that the airspeed remained stable without continuous control input.
texts.4: SP accelerated the A/C to the standard climb airspeed on schedule and maintained it with negligible deviation. The pitch attitude required for the climb airspeed was identified quickly and held, and trim was set so that the aircraft flew the target airspeed hands-light. No airspeed oscillation was present at any point in the departure.
texts.marginal: SP accelerated to and maintained the proper climb airspeed inside the required tolerance, but the airspeed oscillated slowly around the standard and each correction was made a step behind the trend. No prompting was needed and the airspeed never left the standard. SP is expected to fly the known pitch attitude for the climb airspeed and trim early, so that the airspeed is held rather than chased.

error_modes.label: Transition to instrument references and cross-check after liftoff

texts.0: SP, due to a false attitude perception that was not resolved against the instruments, did not transition to the flight instruments at the briefed point after liftoff and did not maintain the proper climbing attitude by reference to them. Attitude and heading were flown on outside cues until the airspeed diverged more than 10 knots from the standard, outside the -0,+10 knots tolerance, and the departure track was lost. IP intervened, took the controls and re-established the climb on instruments.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed instrument transition after liftoff, did not establish the instrument cross-check before the outside references were lost. Attitude control degraded until the airspeed reached about 10 knots off the standard, at the limit of the -0,+10 knots tolerance, and the parameters were recovered only after the IP called the required instrument indications.
texts.2: SP, due to an instrument cross-check that remained fixed on the attitude indication for several seconds after liftoff, did not include the airspeed and heading references in the scan at the briefed point. The airspeed deviation reached roughly 7 knots and the heading drifted off the departure track, between the code 3 and code 1 tolerances. SP re-established the full cross-check on his own and returned the parameters to the standard without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP transitioned to the flight instruments immediately at liftoff and maintained a continuous cross-check of attitude, airspeed, altitude and heading. Attitude was controlled by reference to the instruments and the airspeed was held within the -0,+5 knots tolerance while the departure track was flown accurately.
texts.4: SP transitioned to the flight instruments at liftoff with no interruption in aircraft control and maintained a systematic cross-check throughout the departure. Attitude, airspeed, altitude and heading were kept with negligible deviation, and each control input was made from the instrument indication rather than in reaction to it. The instrument scan was unaffected by the checklist and radio work.
texts.marginal: SP transitioned to the flight instruments after liftoff and held all parameters within standards, but the scan dwelled on the attitude indication and the remaining instruments were sampled at a low rate. No deviation left the standard and no prompting was required. SP is expected to broaden the cross-check rate immediately after liftoff so that airspeed and heading are captured before they move rather than after.

error_modes.label: Torque compensation during takeoff roll at MAX power

texts.0: SP, due to the control stick not being deflected slightly right and the left deviation from power application not being counteracted with right rudder, did not hold the takeoff roll along the centerline as the PCL was advanced to MAX. The aircraft tracked progressively left, lateral displacement passed 10 ft from the runway centerline outside the +/-10 ft tolerance, and the divergence was still increasing at rotation speed. IP intervened on the rudder to re-align the aircraft with the runway.
texts.1: SP, due to right rudder applied late against the left deviation generated by torque at MAX power, did not keep the aircraft on the centerline through the acceleration. Displacement reached about 10 ft left of the centerline, at the limit of the +/-10 ft tolerance, and was corrected only after the IP called for right rudder. The stick was left laterally neutral instead of being deflected slightly right to compensate for torque.
texts.2: SP, due to a right rudder input that lagged the power application, allowed the aircraft to start left as the PCL reached MAX. Displacement grew to roughly 7 ft left of the centerline, between the +/-5 ft and +/-10 ft tolerances, before SP recognized the trend and re-established the track well before rotation speed. No IP input or prompting was required.
texts.3: SP anticipated the left deviation caused by torque at MAX power and counteracted it with right rudder while holding the control stick slightly right. The takeoff roll was tracked within +/-5 ft of the runway centerline from brake release to liftoff. Rudder pressure was adjusted continuously as the power stabilized.
texts.4: SP applied right rudder and slight right stick together with the power advance, so no left deviation developed at MAX power. The centerline was held with negligible displacement throughout the roll and the rudder pressure was reduced smoothly as the flight controls became more effective. Directional control was never disturbed by the engine instrument check at maximum power.
texts.marginal: SP counteracted the torque-induced left deviation and held the takeoff roll inside the centerline tolerance, but the right rudder was applied as a single large correction after the aircraft had already started left. Displacement stayed within the standard and no prompting was required. SP is expected to lead the power application with rudder so that the input is anticipatory rather than a response to a developing deviation.

error_modes.label: Heel position on the rudder pedals during takeoff roll

texts.0: SP, due to the heels being left on the rudder pedals instead of moved to the floor, applied brake pressure while using rudder for directional control during the takeoff roll. The braking was asymmetric, the aircraft yawed and passed 10 ft from the runway centerline outside the +/-10 ft tolerance, and the acceleration towards rotation speed was degraded without the condition being recognized. IP intervened by directing the feet off the brakes and taking the rudder to re-align the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to the heels remaining on the rudder pedals through the takeoff roll, allowed intermittent brake pressure on each directional correction. Displacement reached about 10 ft from the centerline, at the limit of the +/-10 ft tolerance, and the braking stopped only after the IP called the foot position. The heels were not moved to the floor at brake release as briefed.
texts.2: SP, due to a high foot position on the rudder pedals at brake release, touched the brakes on the first directional correction of the takeoff roll. A slight deceleration and a displacement of about 7 ft from the centerline developed, between the +/-5 ft and +/-10 ft tolerances, before SP lowered the heels to the floor and continued on rudder alone. The correction was made without IP intervention and the acceleration was not further affected.
texts.3: SP moved the heels from the rudder pedals to the floor at brake release and used rudder alone for directional control throughout the takeoff roll. No brake pressure was applied, the acceleration was uninterrupted and the aircraft was tracked within +/-5 ft of the centerline.
texts.4: SP placed the heels on the floor before the power was advanced and kept them there for the whole takeoff roll, so directional control was made exclusively with rudder. The acceleration was uninterrupted and lateral displacement was negligible. Foot position was re-checked as part of the pre-takeoff flow rather than after the roll had begun.
texts.marginal: SP used rudder for directional control and no measurable braking occurred, but the heels were lowered to the floor only after the takeoff roll had started. All parameters stayed within the standard and no IP action was required. SP is expected to set the foot position before power is advanced so that no part of the roll is flown with the heels on the pedals.

error_modes.label: Elevator position during takeoff roll and nose gear loading

texts.0: SP, due to forward stick carried through the acceleration instead of the elevator being positioned approximately neutral, loaded the nose gear during the takeoff roll and allowed it to dig in. Directional control degraded with the nose wheel loaded, the aircraft passed 10 ft from the runway centerline outside the +/-10 ft tolerance, and the rotation was made from an unstable track. IP intervened on the controls to unload the nose gear and re-align the takeoff roll.
texts.1: SP, due to the elevator not being held approximately neutral during the takeoff roll, kept the nose gear loaded well past the point where the flight controls had become effective. Track deviation reached about 10 ft, at the limit of the +/-10 ft tolerance, and the stick was released to the neutral position only after the IP called the elevator position.
texts.2: SP, due to a forward stick pressure carried over from the taxi, did not set the elevator approximately neutral at brake release. The nose gear stayed loaded through the early acceleration and the aircraft wandered to roughly 7 ft from the centerline, between the +/-5 ft and +/-10 ft tolerances, before SP neutralized the elevator on his own and steadied the track. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP positioned the elevator approximately neutral at brake release and held it there, so the nose gear was not allowed to dig in during the takeoff roll. Directional control remained precise and the aircraft tracked within +/-5 ft of the centerline until backstick pressure was smoothly applied at rotation speed.
texts.4: SP set the elevator approximately neutral before the power was advanced and maintained that position throughout the acceleration, keeping the nose gear lightly loaded and the aircraft directionally stable. Lateral deviation was negligible and the change from neutral elevator to the smooth backstick pressure at rotation speed was made as one continuous input.
texts.marginal: SP held the elevator close to neutral for the takeoff roll and the nose gear was never allowed to dig in, but small forward pressures reappeared each time SP made a directional correction. Deviations remained within the standard and no prompting was needed. SP is expected to isolate the pitch and rudder inputs so that elevator position is not disturbed by directional corrections.

error_modes.label: Reduction of control input size as airspeed increases

texts.0: SP, due to control inputs that were not progressively reduced as the flight controls became more effective with increasing airspeed, over-controlled the aircraft in the second half of the takeoff roll. The overcorrections built into a lateral oscillation that carried the aircraft more than 10 ft either side of the runway centerline, outside the +/-10 ft tolerance, and it was still oscillating at liftoff. IP intervened on the controls to damp the oscillation and stabilize the takeoff.
texts.1: SP, due to inputs kept at a constant size while the controls became more effective with speed, alternated aileron and rudder corrections through the later takeoff roll. Displacement swung to about 10 ft either side of the centerline, at the limit of the +/-10 ft tolerance, and the oscillation stopped only after the IP called for smaller inputs.
texts.2: SP, due to a correction sized for low speed being applied after the controls had become more effective, overshot the centerline once during the acceleration. Displacement reached roughly 7 ft on the opposite side, between the +/-5 ft and +/-10 ft tolerances, and SP immediately reduced the size of the following inputs and settled the track before rotation without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP progressively reduced the size of the control inputs as airspeed increased and the flight controls became more effective. No overcorrection developed and the aircraft was held within +/-5 ft of the centerline through to liftoff. Corrections were flown as control pressures rather than as displacements of stick and rudder.
texts.4: SP matched every correction to the control effectiveness available at that airspeed, so the inputs became smaller and smoother as the takeoff roll progressed. Lateral deviation was negligible and no correction had to be taken back out. The same input discipline was carried through the rotation and into the initial climb.
texts.marginal: SP reduced the input size as the airspeed increased and remained within the centerline tolerance, but two corrections were still larger than required and had to be partially removed. No deviation left the standard and the IP made no calls. SP is expected to move to control pressures earlier in the roll so that no input needs to be reversed.

error_modes.label: Aileron into the crosswind and prevention of skipping

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient aileron held into the wind, allowed the upwind wing to develop more lift and begin flying before the downwind wing during the crosswind takeoff roll. The aircraft skipped in a series of small bounces, moved sideways more than 10 ft from the runway centerline outside the +/-10 ft tolerance, and the landing gear was stressed laterally without the condition being recognized. IP intervened on the controls to place aileron into the wind and stop the skipping.
texts.1: SP, due to aileron applied into the wind only after the upwind wing had already started to rise, did not keep the wings level during the crosswind takeoff roll. The aircraft skipped once and moved sideways to about 10 ft from the centerline, at the limit of the +/-10 ft tolerance, and the correct deflection was set only after the IP called for stick into the wind.
texts.2: SP, due to aileron that was not prepositioned into the wind before brake release, was late in matching the deflection to the crosswind component in the early takeoff roll. The upwind wing became light and the aircraft drifted to roughly 7 ft downwind of the centerline, between the +/-5 ft and +/-10 ft tolerances, before SP increased the aileron on his own and re-established the track. No skipping developed and no IP input was needed.
texts.3: SP anticipated the aileron requirement due to the crosswind, prepositioned the stick into the wind and adjusted the deflection as required during the takeoff roll. The wings were held level, the upwind wing was not allowed to rise and no skipping occurred, with the aircraft tracking within +/-5 ft of the centerline.
texts.4: SP set aileron into the wind before brake release and reduced the deflection progressively as the controls became more effective, so the wings stayed level for the whole crosswind takeoff roll. The upwind wing never became light, no sideways movement or gear loading occurred and lateral deviation was negligible. Rudder was used in parallel to keep the aircraft from weather-vaning.
texts.marginal: SP held aileron into the wind and prevented the upwind wing from rising, but the deflection was established after brake release instead of being prepositioned and was then adjusted in noticeable steps. The wings stayed level and the track remained within the standard. SP is expected to preposition the aileron for the reported crosswind so that the first correction of the roll is not a catch-up input.

error_modes.label: Release of crosswind controls after liftoff and crab into the wind

texts.0: SP, due to the crosswind controls being held after takeoff instead of released, did not allow the aircraft to crab into the wind and let the upwind wing dip towards the ground. The climb was flown uncoordinated, runway alignment on the takeoff leg was lost and the airspeed diverged more than 10 knots from the standard, outside the -0,+10 knots tolerance. IP intervened on the controls to level the wings and establish the crab.
texts.1: SP, due to aileron and rudder held into the wind after the wheels left the ground, did not release the crosswind controls on becoming airborne. The upwind wing dropped and the aircraft was displaced downwind of the runway alignment while the airspeed reached about 10 knots off the standard, at the limit of the -0,+10 knots tolerance, and the wings were levelled only after the IP called for the controls to be released.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed release of the crosswind controls, carried the into-wind deflection for several seconds after liftoff. Drift off the takeoff leg alignment began and the airspeed moved about 7 knots from the standard, between the -0,+5 and -0,+10 knots tolerances, before SP neutralized the controls, allowed the aircraft to crab into the wind and restored coordinated flight without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP released the crosswind controls after takeoff and allowed the aircraft to crab into the wind, adjusting rudder as the wheels left the ground and the airspeed increased. The upwind wing was not allowed to dip, the climb was flown in coordinated flight and runway alignment on the takeoff leg was maintained with the airspeed inside the -0,+5 knots tolerance.
texts.4: SP blended the release of the crosswind controls with the liftoff, so the aircraft crabbed into the wind with no wing drop and no yaw excursion. Coordinated flight was maintained with the ball centered, runway alignment on the takeoff leg was held precisely and the airspeed deviation was negligible. The changing rudder requirement was trimmed out rather than held on pressure.
texts.marginal: SP released the crosswind controls after takeoff and held runway alignment on the takeoff leg, but the release was made as one abrupt movement and a small wing drop and yaw had to be corrected. All parameters stayed within the standard and no prompting was required. SP is expected to release the crosswind inputs progressively as the wheels leave the ground so that the crab is established without a transient.

error_modes.label: Trim after liftoff for adverse yaw and increasing airspeed

texts.0: SP, due to no right rudder trim being applied after takeoff and safe gear retraction and no nose-down trim as the airspeed increased, flew the climb with adverse yaw uncorrected and continuous pressure on the control stick. The ball stayed off center and the out-of-trim pitch pressure let the airspeed diverge more than 10 knots from the standard, outside the -0,+10 knots tolerance, while heading control on the departure leg degraded. IP intervened on the controls and reset the trim before the departure was continued.
texts.1: SP, due to the trim not being reset after gear retraction, flew the climb on control pressures alone. Adverse yaw was left uncorrected with the ball off center and the airspeed reached about 10 knots off the standard, at the limit of the -0,+10 knots tolerance, before the IP called for right rudder trim and nose-down trim.
texts.2: SP, due to trim inputs made only after the control pressures had built up, climbed out of trim through the first part of the departure leg. The ball was displaced and the airspeed drifted about 7 knots from the standard, between the -0,+5 and -0,+10 knots tolerances, until SP applied right rudder trim and nose-down trim on his own and stabilized the climb. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP applied some right rudder trim immediately after takeoff and safe gear retraction to counteract adverse yaw and center the ball, and applied nose-down trim as the airspeed increased. Control pressures were relieved, the climb was flown coordinated and the airspeed was held within the -0,+5 knots tolerance.
texts.4: SP trimmed in rudder and pitch continuously through the acceleration, so the aircraft was flown with negligible control pressure from immediately after gear retraction. The ball stayed centered, airspeed and heading deviations were negligible, and the trim work was fitted around the cleanup checks without interrupting the instrument cross-check.
texts.marginal: SP set right rudder trim and nose-down trim after liftoff and held all parameters within standards, but the trim lagged the acceleration and residual stick pressure was carried for part of the climb. The ball was only slightly off center and no prompting was required. SP is expected to trim continuously as the airspeed changes so that the aircraft is not flown against sustained control pressure.

error_modes.label: Gates for the first turn after takeoff

texts.0: SP, due to a turn started before the minimum of 140 KIAS and 400 feet AGL was reached and without being otherwise directed, did not climb straight ahead to the required gates after liftoff. Bank was applied with the airspeed more than 10 knots short of the turn gate and with the climb not verified on the altimeter and VSI, a deviation outside the applicable 10 knot tolerance, and the departure was flown from a low energy state. IP intervened on the controls to roll the wings level and continue the straight climb to the gates.
texts.1: SP, due to an early bank input on the departure leg, started the turn about 10 knots short of the 140 KIAS gate and below 400 feet AGL. The shortfall was at the limit of the applicable 10 knot tolerance and the wings were rolled level only after the IP called the gates. SP had not verified the climb with the altimeter and VSI before initiating the turn.
texts.2: SP, due to attention shifting to the departure heading before the gates were confirmed, began to bank with the airspeed roughly 7 knots short of 140 KIAS. The deviation stayed between the 5 and 10 knot tolerances and SP recognized the shortfall, levelled the wings and completed the straight climb to 140 KIAS and 400 feet AGL before turning, with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP climbed straight ahead after liftoff and did not turn until the aircraft was at a minimum of 140 KIAS and 400 feet AGL. The climb was verified on the altimeter and VSI before bank was applied and the airspeed at the start of the turn was within the 5 knot tolerance of the standard.
texts.4: SP maintained the initial attitude until the target climb speed, verified the climb on the altimeter and VSI and started the first turn only after both the 140 KIAS and 400 feet AGL gates were met. Airspeed and altitude at the gates were achieved with negligible deviation and the roll into the departure turn cost no climb rate.
texts.marginal: SP delayed the first turn until 140 KIAS and 400 feet AGL were met, but the gates were confirmed only as the bank was being set up and the airspeed was marginally above the minimum. No standard was exceeded and no IP call was needed. SP is expected to confirm both gates on the instruments before the turn is initiated, so that the margin above 140 KIAS is not reduced to the minimum.
